topic_tag: a rural poet and her brother in the city
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
blank_sentence: Her biographer describes the brother, in the end, as the poet's ______.

worlds.passage: For forty years a poet lived on her family's farm, two days' ride from the city where her younger brother lived and where her books were printed. When the farm failed in 1880, he paid off its debts. From then on a draft on his bank reached the farm on the first of every month, and she gave up the village teaching that had left her no hours to write. Nearly all of her published poems date from after 1880. Her biographer describes the brother, in the end, as the poet's ______.
worlds.explanation: He cleared the farm's debts, then sent money monthly, which let her quit the teaching that had kept her from writing, and the poems followed, so he was the poet's "benefactor." "Critic" fails because his effect on the poems runs through her freed time, and nothing says he judged them; "courier" fails because what travels is his money to her, not her poems to the city; "confidant" fails because the tie described is financial support, with no private matters shared.

critic.why: His effect on her poetry is through giving her time to write, not through judging what she wrote.

courier.quote: a draft on his bank reached the farm
courier.why: What moves between them is his money to her, not her poems to the printer.

confidant.why: His role is paying for her life and time, not hearing what she told no one else.

worlds.passage: For forty years a poet lived on her family's farm, two days' ride from the city where her younger brother lived and where her books were printed. The weekly letters she wrote him are the only place her doubts about her marriage appear; her diaries never mention them. No one else seems to have known of her decision in 1885 to stop publishing, which he first spoke of at her funeral. Her biographer describes the brother, in the end, as the poet's ______.
worlds.explanation: Her private doubts appear only in letters to him, and he alone knew of her decision and kept it until her death, so he was the poet's "confidant." "Critic" fails because what reached him was her private life, not poems to judge; "courier" fails because what she told him went no further; "benefactor" fails because nothing passes from him to her but his silence, with no money or support described.

critic.why: What he hears is private matters, not poems to judge.

courier.quote: first spoke of at her funeral
courier.why: What reached him went no further while she lived, so he carried nothing on to anyone.

benefactor.quote: The weekly letters she wrote him
benefactor.why: His place in her life is as the one she writes to, not as one who supports her materially.

worlds.passage: For forty years a poet lived on her family's farm, two days' ride from the city where her younger brother lived and where her books were printed. She would not travel and distrusted the mail. Every spring he rode out to the farm and back, and within a week of each return the printer had the year's poems; her proofs came in the summer, the week after his second visit. Her biographer describes the brother, in the end, as the poet's ______.
worlds.explanation: She neither traveled nor used the mail, yet her poems reached the printer just after each of his trips back from the farm, and her proofs just after his next visit, so he carried them: he was the poet's "courier." "Critic" fails because nothing says he judged the poems, only that they arrived; "confidant" fails because what he moved was her finished work, not anything she told him; "benefactor" fails because no money or support is described.

critic.quote: within a week of each return
critic.why: His role is timed to the poems' arrival at the printer; nothing involves judging them.

confidant.why: The problem he solves is getting her work to the city, not hearing private matters.

benefactor.quote: rode out to the farm and back
benefactor.why: His service is the journey, not financial help.

worlds.passage: For forty years a poet lived on her family's farm, two days' ride from the city where her younger brother lived and where her books were printed. He edited a literary weekly there, and each of her books was discussed in it within a month of appearing, in unsigned columns that quoted her weakest lines. Her later notebooks show her reworking exactly the poems those columns had faulted, and the weekly's records name its editor as the author of every one of them. Her biographer describes the brother, in the end, as the poet's ______.
worlds.explanation: The unsigned columns that faulted her lines turn out to be his, and she revised where they found fault, so he was the poet's "critic." "Courier" fails because he met her books only after they were printed; "confidant" fails because his judgments were public columns, not private matters she told him; "benefactor" fails because no money or support passes between them.

courier.why: He deals with her books after publication, so he is not the one delivering them.

confidant.why: His comments were printed for the public, not private confidences between them.

benefactor.why: What he offers is judgment of her poems, not material support.
